rewrites.prompt: A Walvis Bay fishing company has raised its catch per vessel this season by taking more hake than the stock can replace. Explain the difference between productivity and sustainability as tests of this operation.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Productivity measures output per unit of input over a stated period, so it says how hard the inputs are working now; sustainability asks whether the operation can be carried on into the long term, using natural resources no faster than they are replaced. The fishing company's higher catch per vessel is a rise in productivity this season. But taking more hake than the stock replaces is a fall in sustainability: the same catch cannot be repeated in later seasons, so this season's productivity gain may be followed by smaller catches, idle vessels and lost jobs.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - a ratio for the period against the ability to repeat the period.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the fishing company - catch per vessel up this season while the stock is run down; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the time horizon; the two can move in opposite directions.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Rundu clinic sees ninety patients a day at a low cost per patient, but many are sent away without the right treatment. Explain the difference between efficiency and effectiveness at this clinic.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Efficiency asks about the ratio of output to the resources used; effectiveness asks whether the intended result was reached. The clinic is efficient: ninety patients a day at a low cost per patient means few resources for each unit of output. It is not effective: its objective is patients correctly treated, and many leave without the right treatment. Because the two are different questions, improving one does not settle the other - a clinic that treated everybody correctly by keeping three times the staff it needed would be effective but inefficient.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - what is measured: resources per unit of output against whether the objective was met.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the clinic - efficient but ineffective, with a reason for each; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: a difference in what is measured, not in degree.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: An Okahandja factory produces 2 000 units a week with 20 employees. It adds a night shift of 10 people, and weekly output rises to 2 700 units. Explain the difference between production and productivity, using these figures.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Production is the total quantity produced in a period; productivity is that quantity divided by the input used to produce it. The factory's production has risen from 2 000 to 2 700 units a week. Its labour productivity has fallen: 2 000 / 20 = 100 units per employee before, and 2 700 / 30 = 90 units per employee after, because the night shift produces less per person than the day shift. Reporting only the 2 700 units would hide that each employee is now producing less.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - a total against a ratio.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the factory's figures - production up to 2 700 while productivity falls from 100 to 90 units per employee; 1 mark if only one figure is worked.
Boundary: total against ratio, shown moving in opposite directions.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek bakery makes 600 brown loaves, cleans its equipment, then makes 400 white loaves. A Namibian water bottler fills the same bottle on one line all week. Explain the difference between batch and flow production, using these two operations.
rewrites.canonical_answer: In batch production a group of identical items completes one stage together before the whole group moves on, and the equipment is reset between groups; in flow production items move continuously through a fixed sequence of stages and nothing is reset. The bakery is batching: each run of loaves stops for a clean-down, which lets it offer several breads with modest equipment, at the price of time lost at each change. The bottler is using flow: its line does not stop for changeovers, giving a very low cost per bottle at high volume, but it needed a large outlay and allows almost no variety.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - items moving as a group with resets against items moving continuously without them.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the bakery and the bottler on the same dimensions - variety, capital, set-up time; 1 mark if only one is applied.
Boundary: stated before the consequences.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A private clinic in Windhoek sees patients, runs tests in its own laboratory and dispenses medicines. Explain one way in which its transformational process differs from a factory's.
rewrites.canonical_answer: The clinic's key input is the patient, and its transformation changes the patient's condition rather than the form of a material, as a factory's does. Because the customer is inside the process, the clinic cannot produce in advance or hold its output in stock: a consultation or a test happens only when the patient is there. So it has to match doctors, nurses and laboratory capacity to when patients arrive, whereas a factory can build up stock in quiet weeks and sell it later.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the patient is an input, and the transformation changes the patient rather than a material.

2 marks (AO2): the reasoning applied to the clinic - because the customer is inside the process, the work cannot be done in advance or stocked, so capacity must match arrivals; 1 mark for a generic services point.
Context: the clinic's own facts. Conclusion: a clear difference from the factory case.
rewrites.why: Describe is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks and narrowed to the one difference the card was built to teach - the customer as an input.

rewrites.prompt: A commercial laundry in Swakopmund uses 14 litres of water and N$6 of purchased power for every kilogram of washing, in a town where water is trucked in and rationed in dry years. Explain why a measure that cuts its water use per kilogram matters more here than it would for a laundry in a coastal city with abundant supply.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A measure such as filtering and re-using rinse water cuts the litres used per kilogram without changing the output. In Swakopmund the constraint is physical as well as financial: where water is trucked in and rationed in dry years, the quantity available sets a ceiling on how much washing the laundry can do at all. So cutting litres per kilogram raises the output it can produce from its permitted supply, not just the cost of that output. In a city with abundant water the same measure would only save money, and its case would rest on the water price against the cost of the filtration plant.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the point identified - a water-saving measure cuts litres per kilogram, and here water is a physical limit on output.

2 marks (AO2): the reasoning applied - because supply is trucked in and rationed, the saving raises the output possible, whereas with abundant supply it only lowers cost; 1 mark for water saving in general.
Context: the rationing in this town. Conclusion: the comparison with the abundant-supply case drawn explicitly.
rewrites.why: Suggest is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks, keeping the point the card teaches - why the water measure matters more in this town.

rewrites.prompt: Define labour productivity, giving its formula and the units in which it is measured.
marking_guidance: 2 marks (AO1): a precise definition with the formula the right way up - total output in a period divided by the number of employees in that period - and its units; 1 mark for partial understanding.
Precise meaning only: the units and the stated period are part of the definition.
rewrites.why: State is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Define at 2 marks, a definition carrying its formula and units.
